items.question: Trace the evolution of India's industrial policy from 1948 to 1991. How did the New Industrial Policy of 1991 transform the industrial landscape of the country?
items.modelAnswer:
India's industrial policy has evolved from a **state-led, controlled model** to a **liberalised, market-oriented one**. The **Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948**, the first of its kind, accepted a **mixed economy** in which the state entered key industries while leaving space for private enterprise. The **IPR of 1956** — often called the **'economic constitution of India'** — gave effect to the **socialist pattern of society** and the **Mahalanobis-based Second Five Year Plan**; it classified industries into **Schedule A** (17 industries exclusively for the state), **Schedule B** (state supplemented by private effort) and **Schedule C** (left to the private sector), giving the public sector the 'commanding heights'. Subsequent policies (1977, 1980) refined small-industry promotion and capacity utilisation but retained the **licence-permit raj**, which bred inefficiency, capital-output lags and limited competition.

The **New Industrial Policy of 1991**, launched amid a **balance-of-payments crisis** and as part of the **LPG reforms**, marked a decisive break. It **abolished industrial licensing** for all but a short list of industries, **reduced the industries reserved for the public sector from 17 to 8** (today just two — atomic energy and railway operations), **liberalised FDI** and technology imports, diluted the **MRTP Act** (later replaced by the **Competition Act, 2002**), and initiated **disinvestment** of public-sector equity.

The transformation was far-reaching: private and foreign investment surged, competition and efficiency improved, the **services and manufacturing base diversified**, and India integrated with the global economy. Yet challenges persisted — **jobless growth**, regional imbalance, and a **manufacturing share stuck below the ~25% target** set by later initiatives like Make in India. Thus 1991 shifted the state's role from **producer to facilitator and regulator**, laying the foundation for the reform-era industrial economy.
keyPoints: IPR 1948 — first policy, mixed economy; state plus private roles.
IPR 1956 — 'economic constitution', socialist pattern, Second Plan; Schedules A/B/C with public sector on the commanding heights.
Pre-1991 licence-permit raj bred inefficiency and limited competition.
NIP 1991: abolished most licensing, cut reserved public-sector industries 17→8 (now 2), liberalised FDI, MRTP→Competition Act 2002, began disinvestment.
Impact: rising investment, competition, diversification and global integration; state shifts from producer to facilitator.
Persisting challenges: jobless growth, regional imbalance, low manufacturing GDP share.
items.source: NCERT Indian Economic Development; DPIIT industrial policy history

items.question: Discuss the recent initiatives taken by the Government of India to boost manufacturing and industrial growth. In this context, examine the role of industrial corridors in the development of Andhra Pradesh.
items.modelAnswer:
To reverse a stagnant manufacturing share and generate jobs, the government has launched a cluster of **supply-side and investment-oriented initiatives**. **Make in India (2014)** seeks to make the country a global manufacturing hub across 25 sectors, targeting a **~25% manufacturing share of GDP**. The **Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes (2020)** reward **incremental domestic production** across **14 sectors** — electronics, pharma, autos, telecom, textiles, solar PV and more — with an outlay of about **₹1.97 lakh crore**, aiming to build scale and cut imports. **Startup India** and **Standup India** (both 2016) nurture innovation and inclusive entrepreneurship, while the **revised MSME classification** (composite investment-and-turnover criteria, with limits enhanced from 1 April 2025) enables firms to grow without losing benefits. Structural reforms include the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016** for time-bound exit, and the **four labour codes** — consolidating 29 central laws — which **came into force on 21 November 2025** and extend social security to gig and platform workers. Infrastructure is supported through **SEZs**, **NIMZs** and **industrial corridors** such as the DMIC and the East Coast Economic Corridor.

For **Andhra Pradesh**, corridors are central to industrial strategy. The **Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor (VCIC)** is the **first phase of the East Coast Economic Corridor (ECEC)**, India's **first coastal economic corridor**, developed with the **Asian Development Bank** as lead partner. Running ~800 km through several AP districts and aligned with the **Golden Quadrilateral**, it leverages the state's **long coastline, ports (Visakhapatnam) and Act East** location to attract manufacturing in electronics, pharma and food processing. The **AP Industrial Development Policy** complements this by developing investment nodes such as **Sri City, Kopparthi (Kadapa) and Orvakal (Kurnool)** and offering single-window clearances and incentives.

Collectively these measures can raise industrial output, exports and quality jobs; their success, however, depends on **stable policy, land and power availability, skilling and last-mile infrastructure** — areas where AP's coastal-corridor model offers a promising template.
keyPoints: Make in India (2014): global manufacturing hub, 25 sectors, ~25% GDP-share target.
PLI (2020): incentives on incremental production across 14 sectors, ~₹1.97 lakh crore outlay.
Startup/Standup India (2016) and revised MSME classification (enhanced limits from 1 Apr 2025).
Structural reforms: IBC 2016; four labour codes consolidating 29 laws, in force 21 Nov 2025.
Infrastructure: SEZs, NIMZs and corridors (DMIC, ECEC).
AP: VCIC is the first phase of the ECEC (India's first coastal corridor), ADB-led, ~800 km through AP along the Golden Quadrilateral.
AP Industrial Development Policy develops nodes like Sri City, Kopparthi and Orvakal with single-window incentives.
Success depends on stable policy, land/power, skilling and last-mile infrastructure.
items.source: DPIIT — Make in India, PLI; Ministry of MSME; Ministry of Labour (labour codes 2025); ADB / Government of Andhra Pradesh — VCIC
